chunks: That was narrated - Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from al-Hajjāl from Hammād ibn 'Uthmān from Abū Baṣīr from Abū 'Abdillāh (peace be upon him) who said:
It is appropriate for the Imam to let those behind him hear everything he says, and it is not appropriate for those behind him to let him hear anything of what they say.
And it is not permissible for one who follows the Imam to pray 'Asr with him if he has not yet prayed 'Dhuhr.
83 That was narrated - Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from 'Ali ibn al-Hakam from Sulaym al-Farrā' who said:

I asked him about a man who is the mu'adhdhin and Imam of a people, who is on the way to Mecca or elsewhere, and he prays 'Asr with them in its time. A man who does not know enters and thinks it is the first prayer (Dhuhr). Is it sufficient for him that it is 'Asr? He said, 'No.'
84 And as for what was narrated - al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Hammād ibn 'Uthmān who said:
I asked Abū 'Abdillāh (peace be upon him) about a man who leads a people in prayer and prays 'Asr while it is Dhuhr for them. He said, 'It is sufficient for him and sufficient for them.'

This does not contradict what we mentioned earlier, because it is sufficient for him and for them only if he does not bind his prayer to their prayer, and he intends for himself the prayer of 'Asr, and they intend for themselves the prayer of Dhuhr, and they are not following him in the intention of the prayer. And whenever the matter is as we mentioned, their prayer is valid.
ai.seo_question: What are the rules for an Imam and congregation when they have different prayer intentions or times?
ai.summary: This passage from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the jurisprudential nuances of congregational prayer, emphasizing the acoustic hierarchy where the Imam’s recitation is audible to followers, but not vice versa. It resolves apparent contradictions regarding praying 'Asr when Dhuhr is intended by distinguishing between strict following (where intentions must align) and independent prayer behind an Imam (where distinct intentions allow validity for both), reflecting the Shia emphasis on the precision of *niyyah* in ritual acts.
